rewrite.description: Compiled from 1969 club shows in Dallas and San Francisco, this double album catches the post-Cale lineup stretching songs well past their studio lengths, with long, patient versions of 'Heroin' and 'Ocean'. The performances are looser and warmer than the studio takes, Lou Reed's conversational vocals riding a band clearly comfortable playing for a small room. It is for listeners who want the Velvets as a working club band rather than an art project.
rewrite.lineage: Its long, exploratory live arrangements sound like a forerunner of the extended guitar jamming that Yo La Tengo and Sonic Youth would later build whole albums around.

rewrite.description: Assembled from tracks the band recorded in 1968-69 for a shelved fourth MGM album, VU surfaced from the Polygram vaults over a decade after the band split and reveals a more accessible, straightforwardly melodic Velvet Underground than the finished albums suggested. Songs like 'Stephanie Says' and 'Ocean' are sung by Lou Reed in a warm, conversational register over clean, lightly strummed guitars. Several tracks here were later reworked by Reed on his solo albums, making this a good place to hear them in their leaner original form.
rewrite.lineage: A vault release that filled in the melodic, song-oriented side of the Velvets' catalog; several of its songs were later reworked on Lou Reed's solo records.

problems: 'Ocean' is not on this album (it is on VU)
key track 'I Can't Stand It' is from VU, not Another View

rewrite.description: The leftover half of the same 1968-69 vault material that produced VU the year before, Another View is rawer and more scattered, pairing two versions of the drifting 'Hey Mr. Rain' with rough outtakes closer in spirit to White Light/White Heat. 'Ride Into the Sun' would later resurface, reworked, on Lou Reed's solo debut, and an early 'Rock and Roll' shows the band sketching a song they finished on Loaded. It is a scrappier listen than its companion volume, mainly for listeners who have exhausted the main albums.

Produced by David Bowie and Mick Ronson at the height of glam, Transformer wraps Lou Reed's deadpan tales of Warhol Factory hangers-on in string arrangements, saxophone, and hooky, almost cabaret-pop melodies. 'Walk on the Wild Side' turns a list of drag queens and hustlers into a loping, bass-led single, while 'Perfect Day' and 'Satellite of Love' soften Reed's sneer into genuine tenderness. It is the most approachable door into his solo catalog, for listeners who like their outsider New York portraits dressed in glam-pop gloss.
rewrite.lineage: Takes the Velvet Underground's deadpan character sketches and dresses them in glam-pop production by Bowie and Ronson; later art-pop and indie songwriters who mine outsider characters for empathy sound indebted to it.

rewrite.description: An hour of layered guitar feedback with no beat, melody, or vocal, Metal Machine Music was built by Lou Reed from amplifiers and effects set against each other and left to howl. RCA released it as though it were a rock record and it baffled most listeners, but its shifting overtones sit closer to minimalist drone composition than to anything on the pop charts. It is the most extreme extrapolation of the feedback experiments the Velvet Underground began on White Light/White Heat, for noise and drone listeners only.
rewrite.lineage: Carries the Velvet Underground's feedback drone to its logical, songless extreme, and noise and drone musicians have long claimed it as an early precedent for pure guitar noise as music.

rewrite.description: After the confrontational Metal Machine Music, Coney Island Baby finds Reed unexpectedly tender, singing plainly over warm, unhurried electric and acoustic guitar interplay on songs like 'She's My Best Friend'. The long title track closes the record with a rambling, half-spoken monologue about wanting to play football for the coach, one of Reed's most disarmingly sincere vocal performances. It trades provocation for a hushed, late-night warmth, for listeners who prefer Reed romantic rather than confrontational.
rewrite.lineage: Shows the deadpan Velvet Underground storyteller turning inward toward quiet sincerity, a mode that hushed, plainspoken songwriters like Smog and Bill Callahan sound indebted to.

problems: overdose section is not the closing verse

rewrite.description: Street Hassle mixes studio takes with live band recordings made using an early binaural technique, giving the record an unusually spatial, in-the-room feel. The eleven-minute title suite splices three linked stories over a looping cello figure, taking in a grim overdose tale and a brief spoken cameo from Bruce Springsteen. It is one of Reed's most structurally ambitious solo pieces, matching punk's rawness to novelistic, multi-part songwriting.
rewrite.lineage: Reed's most punk-adjacent solo record, made as the CBGB scene the Velvets had helped inspire was breaking; its blunt, live-sounding production and long-form storytelling sound like a forerunner of art-punk and slowcore alike.

rewrite.description: Reed's sharpest solo album in years pairs him with guitarist Robert Quine, whose jagged, wiry lead lines spar with Reed's own rhythm guitar on sparse, live-sounding arrangements. Songs like 'The Blue Mask' and 'Waves of Fear' turn confessional, sometimes violent imagery into tense rock, while 'Heavenly Arms' is a plain, unguarded love song. The interplay between the two guitarists gives the record a raw, conversational energy closer to CBGB than to Reed's glossier late-'70s work.
rewrite.lineage: Robert Quine, formerly of Richard Hell and the Voidoids, brought the downtown New York punk guitar vocabulary the Velvet Underground had helped seed back into Reed's solo sound.

rewrite.description: A deliberately stripped-down, two-guitars-bass-drums record, New York is Reed's state-of-the-city address, fourteen songs of blunt social commentary about AIDS, racism, and political corruption meant to be heard start to finish. 'Dirty Blvd.' and 'Romeo Had Juliette' pair plainspoken, almost journalistic lyrics with unfussy, live-sounding guitar rock, a return to directness after a decade of more polished records. It is the latter-day Reed album for listeners who want the unglamorous street detail of the first Velvet Underground record.
rewrite.lineage: Returns to the plain-spoken, street-level songwriting of the first Velvet Underground album, and its bare productions sound like a template for later songwriters who let lyrics, not arrangement, carry a record.

problems: Cale arranged but did not produce (Frazier Mohawk produced)
'permanently out of tune' and recorded-alone claims unverified

rewrite.description: Arranged by John Cale, The Marble Index abandons Chelsea Girl's folk-pop entirely for Nico's own droning harmonium and Cale's stark, dissonant instrumental settings built around her voice and keyboard. Her voice is a flat, doom-laden drone across songs like 'Frozen Warnings', the tempos glacial and the mood bleak throughout. Commercially ignored at the time, it now sounds like a precursor of goth and dark-ambient songwriting, arriving years before those genres had names.
rewrite.lineage: John Cale's arrangements carry the Velvet Underground's drone directly into stark solo songwriting; the record sounds like a root of gothic rock and of the slow, glacial end of slowcore.

problems: Marble Index was not Cale-produced, so 'second Cale-produced' is wrong
Brian Jones dedication, sales and cover claims unverified

rewrite.description: Co-produced by John Cale, Desertshore keeps the harmonium drone of The Marble Index but frames it in slightly warmer, more folk-adjacent arrangements, with Cale supplying much of the surrounding instrumentation. 'Janitor of Lunacy' and 'My Only Child' are sung in Nico's flat, funereal alto with sparse, hushed support that barely rises above a whisper. It is for listeners drawn to bleak, hymn-like stillness rather than songs with hooks.
rewrite.lineage: Continues the Cale-Nico partnership that turned Velvet Underground drone into stark solo song-form; hushed, harmonium- or organ-based indie and slowcore artists sound indebted to that approach.

problems: Morrison-death claim for 'You Forget to Answer' unverified

rewrite.description: Nico's fourth album keeps her harmonium-and-drone sound but folds in synthesizers and electronic textures from Brian Eno, with John Cale producing and Roxy Music's Phil Manzanera adding guitar. The title track is a slow, mournful cover of the Doors' 'The End', sung in Nico's flattened deadpan over a queasy, echoing arrangement. It is the bleakest and most electronically textured of her Cale-era run, for listeners who want drone songwriting at its most desolate.
rewrite.lineage: Extends the Cale/Nico drone sound into early electronic textures, a mix of synth and harmonium drone that later post-punk and dream-pop acts sound indebted to.

rewrite.description: Recorded in the early 1970s partly with John Cale producing but not released until 1976, The Modern Lovers channels Velvet Underground drone, a simple organ-and-bass pulse in the spirit of 'Sister Ray', into deadpan, wide-eyed songs about driving Massachusetts highways at night. Jonathan Richman sings in a flat, enthusiastic near-monotone over Jerry Harrison's droning organ and David Robinson's simple, propulsive drums, raw and all the more direct for it. 'Roadrunner' and 'Pablo Picasso' are the entry points for anyone tracing how punk and indie learned that you didn't need virtuosity.
rewrite.lineage: Richman was an avowed Velvet Underground devotee and John Cale produced some of these sessions; the Sex Pistols later played 'Roadrunner', making the record a documented bridge from the Velvets to punk.

rewrite.description: Back in Your Life leans further into the doo-wop and children's-song influences Jonathan Richman had been exploring since leaving loud electric rock behind, with light, spare backing and plenty of room for his voice. Songs like 'Abdul and Cleopatra' and 'Party in the Woods Tonight' are delivered with the same wide-eyed, unguarded sincerity as his earlier work. It is for listeners who find his innocence charming rather than slight.

I, Jonathan finds Jonathan Richman looking back at his own history, paying tribute to the band he idolized on 'Velvet Underground' and revisiting his most famous song on 'Roadrunner (Twice)'. The arrangements are sparse and unhurried, mostly acoustic guitar and light drums, his voice delivering plain, present-tense observations about parties, summer nights, and dancing on songs like 'That Summer Feeling'. It is a warm, funny entry point to his later catalog for anyone who loves the Modern Lovers.
rewrite.lineage: The song 'Velvet Underground' is an explicit tribute to the band Richman idolized, and the record's loose, unpretentious sound sits close to the 1990s lo-fi and slacker acts that treated him as a touchstone.

rewrite.description: John Cale's solo debut sets the Velvet Underground's drone almost entirely aside for concise, melodic pop, closer to the Byrds or late-'60s Van Morrison than to anything on White Light/White Heat. Cale sings in a warm, unassuming voice over jangling guitars and tight, economical arrangements, songs like 'Big White Cloud' and 'Adelaide' showing off a songwriting craft his avant-garde reputation had obscured. It is the gentlest, most accessible door into his catalog.
rewrite.lineage: Shows the Velvet Underground's classically trained member turning immediately toward pop songcraft, a strand of his work that later jangle and chamber-pop indie bands, drawing equally on drone and melody, sound indebted to.

rewrite.description: Paris 1919 sets John Cale's warm baritone against lush orchestral pop arrangements, filled with references to Dylan Thomas and postwar European history but sung with a deceptively breezy, melodic ease. 'Child's Christmas in Wales' and the title track glide over strings and piano with an almost easy-listening surface that hides genuinely strange, literate lyrics underneath. It is Cale at his most purely melodic, a world away from his viola-drone work in the Velvet Underground but no less carefully constructed.
rewrite.lineage: Applies a Velvet Underground alumnus's classically trained arrangement skill to accessible pop songwriting, a combination that later chamber-pop and orchestral indie acts sound indebted to.

rewrite.description: Produced by John Cale, whose viola drones through the raga-like ten-minute 'We Will Fall', the Stooges' debut otherwise strips rock down to its most primitive elements: simple riffs, Iggy Pop's yowled vocals, and blunt, repetitive song structures built for maximum physical impact. 'I Wanna Be Your Dog' rides a single sleigh-bell-and-three-chord hook, an act of deliberate, defiant primitivism that punk bands would take up a decade later. Cale's involvement is the direct thread tying the album's droning noise back to the Velvet Underground he had just left.

problems: 'most directly cited' and named-band influence unsupported

rewrite.description: Television's debut trades punk's power chords for long, interlocking lead lines between Tom Verlaine and Richard Lloyd, clean, chiming guitar tones with little of the distortion associated with the CBGB scene around them. The title track stretches past ten minutes, the guitars trading solos in a way closer to the Velvet Underground's extended workouts than to the Ramones' three-chord blasts. It is essential for anyone who loves guitar interplay more than guitar volume.
rewrite.lineage: Grew out of the same downtown New York scene the Velvet Underground had helped seed, and its interlocking guitar lines sound like a template for R.E.M., Sonic Youth, and the broader American college-rock guitar vocabulary.

problems: Uncle Tupelo-era underground is context, not documented link

rewrite.lineage: Grew out of Hood and Cooley's earlier Alabama band Adam's House Cat, and sits in the cowpunk and insurgent-country underground that followed Uncle Tupelo; it is the root of the Drive-By Truckers catalog that later took in Jason Isbell.

rewrite.description: DBT's second record keeps the ragged twin-guitar attack but sharpens the storytelling, with songs about backwoods religion, small-time crooks, and bad decisions. Cooley's 'Too Much Sex, Too Little Jesus' and Hood's narrative songs set the template of alternating, contrasting songwriter voices the band would keep for two decades. It's still cheap and fast-sounding, but the character sketches of struggling Southerners are already novelistic.

problems: 'adds' framing for 'Steve McQueen' unverified (song likely predates this live set)

rewrite.description: A raw, sweaty live document capturing the pre-Isbell lineup at full volume in small clubs before the band had much notice outside the South. It reworks songs from the early records into louder, longer versions, with Cooley and Hood trading verses over unpolished, extended guitar solos. It stands as proof of the live reputation that built the band's early word-of-mouth following.

problems: Jason Isbell does not play on Southern Rock Opera (joined after; Rob Malone was third guitarist)

rewrite.description: A sprawling double-concept album that uses the mythology of Lynyrd Skynyrd's 1977 plane crash to tell a bigger story about growing up Southern, torn between pride in the region and shame over its history, the 'duality of the Southern thing'. Hood and Cooley lead a harmonized three-guitar attack that becomes the band's signature, on songs like 'Let There Be Rock' and 'Ronnie and Neil'. It is the record where Drive-By Truckers stop being a scrappy bar band and become the reference point for the whole modern Southern-storytelling-rock lane.
rewrite.lineage: Explicitly built on Lynyrd Skynyrd's story and the Southern-rock tradition, filtered through Uncle Tupelo-style alt-country songwriting; later Southern story-rock from Lucero to Wednesday sounds indebted to it.

problems: 'most fans point to as peak' unsupported

rewrite.description: The first album with Jason Isbell as a full songwriting partner: three distinct voices, Hood, Cooley and Isbell, each contributing character studies of Southern families falling apart. Isbell's title track, about a generations-long family feud, sits next to Cooley's wry 'Marry Me' and Hood's 'Sink Hole', a revenge story narrated by a farmer about to lose his land. The three-guitar interplay is tighter and more melodic than Southern Rock Opera, making this the clearest statement of the band's novelistic, unglamorous approach to the modern South.
rewrite.lineage: Builds on Southern Rock Opera's harmonized three-guitar sound and points directly toward Isbell's own solo career; later story-song bands such as Lucero and American Aquarium sound indebted to its model.

problems: 'Puttin' People on the Moon' is Hood's song, not Cooley's
'The Day John Henry Died' is Isbell's, not Hood's
'Danko/Manuel' is about The Band, not music-business exploitation

rewrite.description: A darker, more explicitly political record about Southern poverty, corruption and violence, built around linked character songs like Hood's 'Puttin' People on the Moon', about hard times in Alabama in the shadow of the space program, and Isbell's 'Danko/Manuel', about the toll the road took on members of The Band. Isbell's 'The Day John Henry Died' reworks the folk legend into a parable about automation and labor. It is heavier and more electric than Decoration Day, pushing the three guitars toward distortion rather than twang.
rewrite.lineage: Extends Decoration Day's three-songwriter structure into more overtly political, working-class territory, a mode that Lee Bains III & the Glory Fires and American Aquarium sound indebted to.

rewrite.description: A shorter, more rock-radio-leaning record made as the band toured constantly and the personal frictions that would soon push Isbell out started to show. It trades some concept-album ambition for tighter, punchier songs like 'Space City' and 'Aftermath USA', though the storytelling instincts stay intact. It shows a band stretching toward a more straightforward rock sound, for listeners who want DBT at its most direct.

rewrite.lineage: The first post-Isbell album, with the band carrying on by expanding Shonna Tucker's role as a third songwriting voice alongside Hood and Cooley.

problems: Jay Gonzalez was already in the band, not newly settling in

rewrite.description: The first album after a three-year studio gap and a lineup shake-up, with Shonna Tucker and John Neff gone and bassist Matt Patton newly aboard, and a return to an even split of Hood and Cooley songs after Cooley had contributed fewer songs for years. Cooley's 'Made Up English Oceans' and 'Primer Coat' are among his sharpest character studies, while Hood's songs turn toward middle-aged reflection. It reasserts the band's two-songwriter-plus-guitars core after a decade of expanding lineups.

problems: 'widely treated as most urgent' critic claim
influence on Lee Bains III/American Aquarium unsupported (Lee Bains predates it)

rewrite.description: An overtly political record made in the year of the 2016 election, tackling police shootings, gun culture and the Confederate flag head-on in songs like Hood's 'What It Means' and Cooley's 'Ramon Casiano'. It trades some of the earlier albums' novelistic distance for direct address, restating the band's long-held position that Southern pride and white supremacy are not the same thing. It is the place to start for listeners who want the band at its most urgent and topical.
rewrite.lineage: Extends The Dirty South's political streak into the present day, sitting alongside younger Southern bands like Lee Bains III & the Glory Fires and American Aquarium that write explicitly about the modern South's politics.

rewrite.description: Written in response to family separations at the border, mass shootings and the Trump years, this is the angriest and most direct record in the catalog, with Hood's 'Thoughts and Prayers' and 'Babies in Cages' naming their targets outright. Hood writes the bulk of the record, with Cooley contributing only a little. It is more topical broadside than character study, a departure from the band's usual novelistic method.

A surprise album released months after The Unraveling, mixing leftover songs from those sessions with new material written during the COVID-19 lockdown and the protests of summer 2020, including the unrest-themed title track. It is looser and more urgent-sounding than a normal studio album, closer to a dispatch from a specific summer than a planned statement. Hood's voice dominates, and the guitars are rough and immediate.

problems: Club XIII dates to Hood and Cooley's 1980s pre-DBT days, not the band's 1990s beginnings

rewrite.description: A loose, funny, nostalgic record looking back at Hood and Cooley's scrappy beginnings playing a Muscle Shoals-area club in their teens and twenties, a deliberate return to warmth and humor after two angry, topical albums. Cooley's 'Every Single Storied Flameout' looks at the touring life, while Hood's title track recalls those earliest gigs by name. It brings back the bar-band energy of the early records decades on, for fans who miss the band's sense of humor.
rewrite.lineage: A full-circle return to the band's own origin story, naming the real Muscle Shoals-area club where Hood and Cooley cut their teeth in the 1980s, long before Southern Rock Opera made them known nationally.

problems: serial-killer song and session-family-history song claims unverified
piano and 'sketchbook for later band songs' claims unverified

rewrite.description: Hood's first solo album is a stark, largely acoustic set of songs that did not fit Drive-By Truckers, recorded quickly and cheaply. It is quieter and more intimate than any DBT record, foregrounding Hood's plainspoken, conversational voice over sparse guitar on songs like the title track and 'Belinda Carlisle Diet'. It plays like a demo-like sketchbook, for fans who want the storyteller without the three-guitar wall.

problems: recording date/shelving story wrong: the album was cut around 2008 with DBT members, not in 2001
lineage tied to wrong pre-SRO period

rewrite.description: Collecting songs Hood had written over many years, some dating back well before Drive-By Truckers took off, Murdering Oscar is a full-band record rather than a solo sketchbook. It sounds closer to a DBT side project than the stripped-down Killers and Stars, with loud guitars and harmony vocals dressing up songs about doomed romance and Southern family history. It is for fans who want more of Hood's dark, funny storytelling in a rowdier setting.
rewrite.lineage: Hood cut it with members of Drive-By Truckers backing him, making it a close cousin of the band's own records.

problems: Hood moved to Portland later (c. 2015), not before this album

rewrite.description: A more atmospheric, reflective solo record with a fuller, more layered band sound than Hood's earlier solo work. Songs like '12:01' and 'Come Back Little Star' deal with aging, loss and looking back, sung in his plainspoken narrative voice over slow-burning guitars. It is for listeners who like Hood's writing but want it quieter and more inward than a Truckers record.
rewrite.lineage: A more produced, band-based follow-up to Killers and Stars, keeping the plainspoken narrative voice Hood uses in Drive-By Truckers.

problems: two-disc format and new/old-material mix unverified

rewrite.description: Hood's most recent solo album continues the plainspoken, personal storytelling of his earlier solo work while looking back on family, age and memory. It keeps the same core method as his prior solo records: narrative verses delivered in his conversational drawl over a full-band arrangement. As his fourth solo album in two decades, it confirms Hood treats his solo work as a slower-moving, more reflective counterpart to Drive-By Truckers.

A solo acoustic live album stripping Drive-By Truckers songs like 'Zip City' and 'Marry Me' down to just Cooley's voice, guitar and dry between-song banter. It highlights Cooley's plainer, funnier, more deadpan songwriting style, since there is no full band arrangement to fill in the space. It is a rare chance to hear the other half of DBT's two-songwriter partnership on his own.

problems: divorce/drinking framing of 'Try' and 'Dress Blues' unsupported; 'Dress Blues' is about a Marine killed in Iraq

rewrite.description: Isbell's solo debut, written largely during his last years in Drive-By Truckers and released shortly after his 2007 departure from the band, with Patterson Hood and other DBT members guesting on several tracks. Songs like 'Try' and 'Dress Blues', about a young Marine from his hometown killed in Iraq, show the same novelistic character-writing he brought to Decoration Day and The Dirty South, now in a warmer, more personal register. It is the clear hinge between his Truckers years and the solo career that found its own lane with Southeastern.

problems: 'last album before polished shift' wrong (Here We Rest followed)

rewrite.description: Isbell's second solo album and the first billed to his new backing band the 400 Unit, made as he settled into life after Drive-By Truckers, with songs like 'Cigarettes and Wine' circling drinking and regret. It keeps the story-song DNA of his Truckers work but with a tight, rock-oriented band of guitars and keyboards behind him. It is for listeners who want Isbell's writing with Southern-rock muscle rather than the quieter polish of his later records.
rewrite.lineage: The formal launch of the 400 Unit as Isbell's backing band, continuing the Southern rock approach of his Drive-By Truckers years before his sound moved toward V7-adjacent territory with Southeastern.

problems: lineage is scene resemblance, not documented

rewrite.description: Lucero's self-titled debut is a raw, road-worn blend of punk energy and country heartbreak from a Memphis band. Ben Nichols' cracked, whiskey-worn voice carries songs about broke-down luck and drinking through heartbreak, closer in spirit to the Replacements than to polished Nashville country. It set the template the band refined over the next two decades: unpretentious, guitar-driven story-songs built for a bar full of people who already know the words.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds like a product of the same Southern punk-to-country pipeline as Slobberbone and Two Cow Garage, with a Drive-By Truckers-like storytelling instinct delivered in a rawer, more punk-rock style.

rewrite.description: Lucero's second album leans further into countryish twang without losing the band's punk backbone, on a record about leaving and coming back to the South. Nichols writes about touring exhaustion and romantic failure in short, direct verses rather than elaborate narrative, closer to a diary than a short story. It shows the band tightening its songwriting while keeping the bar-band grit of the debut.

problems: 'written and recorded during near-constant touring' unverified method claim

rewrite.description: A road album in subject and feel, with songs about the exhaustion and loneliness of life on the highway between shows. It keeps the same scratchy, live-sounding production as the first two records, favoring a full-band, played-live feel over studio polish. Restlessness is the record's throughline, matching a band still building its audience one club date at a time.

problems: 'most often cited by later bands' lineage unsupported

rewrite.description: The record where Lucero's songwriting got sharper without losing its bar-band heart, built around Nichols' cracked, conversational delivery on songs like the title track and 'Sweet Little Thing'. The band starts to sound like a unit rather than a frontman-plus-backing-band, with tighter arrangements and more melodic hooks than the earlier, rougher records. It is where the band's mix of punk toughness and country heartbreak fully clicks, a good first stop for new listeners.
rewrite.lineage: A step up from the road-worn sound of That Much Further West; later alt-country and Southern-rock bands with punk roots sound indebted to this version of Lucero.
Expands on the full-band direction of Nobody's Darlings, moving the group's sound closer to the harmonized-guitar Southern rock of Drive-By Truckers, which it sounds increasingly indebted to.

problems: title is not the address of the studio where it was cut

rewrite.description: Named for a Memphis address tied to the band's history, this is the first Lucero album to add a horn section, pushing the band's sound toward the Memphis soul and Stax tradition alongside its punk and country roots. It is a fuller, more ambitious production than the band's earlier records, without losing Nichols' plainspoken storytelling. It is for listeners who want their bar-band heartbreak with brass and organ behind it.

problems: 'horns permanent' claim contradicted by later records

rewrite.description: A horn-driven, barroom-ready record made after the band signed to ATO, with 'Downtown' capturing the album's mix of bar-band swagger and Memphis soul horns. It is one of Lucero's most purely fun records, built for dancing as much as listening, while still carrying Nichols' plainspoken songwriting about work, love and getting by. It is the pick for listeners who want the band at its loosest and loudest.
rewrite.lineage: Builds directly on the horn arrangements introduced on 1372 Overton Park for the band's ATO Records debut.

rewrite.description: A darker, more atmospheric record, with keyboardist Rick Steff's piano and organ pushed further into the arrangements than on the horn-heavy Women & Work. Nichols' songwriting turns toward distance, family and mortality on tracks like 'Went Looking for Warren Zevon's Los Angeles', trading barroom energy for a heavier, more reflective mood. It shows a band twenty years in still finding new emotional territory rather than repeating itself.

problems: Centro-matic is not a cowpunk act; DBT parallel is resemblance

rewrite.lineage: Came out of the mid-1990s Denton, Texas scene that also produced Centro-matic, and later spun off Brent Best's the Drams; it sounds closely parallel to the Uncle Tupelo-descended insurgent-country movement DBT emerged from in Georgia.

rewrite.description: A louder, more confident follow-up that tightened the band's songwriting while keeping its beer-soaked live energy, with Brent Best's character songs about restless small-town life sharpening into something closer to short fiction. The interplay between rhythm and lead guitars gives the record a rougher, more garage-rock edge than most of the alt-country bands it got lumped in with. It is for listeners who like their twang loud and a little sloppy.
